title: What Made The English Novel Possible
text:
The novel is young. Epic poetry and drama are thousands of years old, but the prose novel as we now recognise it is a creature of the last three hundred years, and it is worth asking what made it possible when it appeared.

Three conditions came together in eighteenth-century Britain. There was a growing town readership with money and leisure. There was cheap print, and a network of circulating libraries, so that a book could be borrowed rather than bought outright. And there was a new appetite for ordinary private life as a subject worth reading about. Earlier prose fiction had dealt in princes and marvels; Defoe and Richardson wrote instead about a castaway counting his supplies and a servant writing letters, in a plain reporting style borrowed from journalism and from the diary. Then the form learned a technique that no earlier kind of storytelling had. Free indirect style lets a narrator slip into a character's thoughts without announcing the move, so that judgement and sympathy can share a single sentence. Austen handled it so naturally that readers still miss the irony on a first pass. Serial publication in the next century did the rest, making novels long, heavily plotted and public.
points: The novel is recent compared with epic and drama, about three hundred years old.
An urban readership with money and leisure grew in eighteenth-century Britain.
Cheap print and circulating libraries meant books could be borrowed rather than bought.
Writers such as Defoe and Richardson took ordinary private life as their subject, in a plain reporting style.
Free indirect style let the narrator enter a character's thoughts, as in Austen's irony.
Serial publication in the nineteenth century made novels long, plotted and public.
